plan: Humanities passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000055), an original first-person essay by a saxophonist on learning to improvise: free versus improvised playing, the conversation analogy, transcription, and a personal voice found by departing from memorized phrases. No jazz passage in the ACT Reading bank. Ten questions, four aimed at hard (meaning of a remark, function of an analogy, a qualified judgment, cause of a change). Plus R054-10 resubmitted as revision 2 on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-R-000054 (stem and key reworded). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Off the Script
passages.text:
When I started playing the saxophone at fourteen, I believed that improvising meant playing whatever came into my head. My teacher, a retired bandleader named Mr. Okafor, let me believe this for exactly one lesson. He put on a recording, told me to play along with "anything you like," and listened while I honked and squealed for three minutes. Then he lifted the needle. "That was free," he said. "It was not improvised."

I did not understand the distinction until much later. Jazz musicians who improvise are not starting from nothing. They are working within a set of chords that repeat beneath the melody, and every note they choose either fits those chords, leans against them, or clashes with them for a moment before resolving. A listener may hear a solo as spontaneous, and it is, but it is spontaneous in the way a conversation is spontaneous: the speakers have not rehearsed their words, yet they share a language whose rules they rarely break by accident.

Mr. Okafor's method for teaching that language was old-fashioned. He had me transcribe solos—listen to a recording of a great saxophonist, slow it down, and write out every note by ear. It took me most of a month to transcribe a single two-minute solo. I complained that I wanted to find my own voice, not copy someone else's. He answered that a voice is built from what it has absorbed, and that nobody ever learned to speak by inventing words.

He was right, though not entirely. After two years of transcribing, I could play convincing imitations of half a dozen musicians, and for a while that was all I could do. My solos were collages of borrowed phrases, stitched together competently and saying nothing in particular. The breakthrough, when it came, was not a matter of learning more. It came on a night when I forgot a phrase I had memorized halfway through playing it and had to find my own way back to the chord. What I played was clumsy. It was also, for the first time, mine.

I teach now, and I still assign transcriptions. But I also tell my students about that night, because I think the lesson runs both ways. Without the language, there is nothing to say. Without the occasional mistake that forces you off the script, there is no one saying it.

passages.title: Making Room for Cars
passages.text:
Passage A

For most of the last century, American cities have required builders to provide a minimum number of parking spaces with every new apartment building, store, and office. The rules were meant to keep cars off crowded streets. Their effects have reached much further. A parking space in a garage can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and that cost is folded into rents and prices whether or not a tenant owns a car. On small or oddly shaped lots, the required spaces can make a project impossible, so the housing is never built at all.

Minimum parking rules also shape how people travel. When every destination promises free parking, driving becomes the easy default, and buses and bike lanes struggle to attract riders. Several cities have recently eliminated their minimums, leaving it to builders to decide how much parking their customers actually want. Builders have not stopped providing parking; they have simply provided less of it in places where residents can walk or take transit. That, rather than any single number written into a code, is how parking ought to be decided.

Passage B

Critics of parking minimums make a strong case, and in dense neighborhoods with frequent trains and buses, I find it persuasive. But most Americans do not live in such places. In a suburb where the nearest bus comes once an hour, a household without parking at home is not a household without a car; it is a household that parks on the street. When a new building is approved without spaces, the cars of its residents do not disappear. They spill onto nearby blocks, where longtime residents, many of whom bought their homes counting on curbside parking, suddenly cannot find a space.

None of this means that the old rules should stay as they are. Many codes demand far more spaces than buildings ever fill. A better approach would be to lower minimums where transit is strong and to tie any remaining requirements to how often buses actually run. Eliminating minimums everywhere at once trades one uniform rule for another, and uniform rules are exactly what got cities into trouble in the first place.

candidates.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Learning to improvise required absorbing a tradition and, eventually, departing from it.
choices.B: Improvisation in jazz is mostly memorized material that is made to sound spontaneous.
choices.C: The narrator's teacher was mistaken to require students to transcribe recorded solos.
choices.D: Jazz is easier to learn than other kinds of music because it has fewer fixed rules.

candidates.evidence: Without the language, there is nothing to say.
candidates.explanation: The narrator learns the language of jazz through transcription, then finds a personal voice only when forced off memorized phrases, and concludes that both are needed.

B.rationale: The narrator calls solos genuinely spontaneous and says the breakthrough came from leaving memorized material.

C.rationale: The narrator says the teacher was right, though not entirely, and still assigns transcriptions.

D.rationale: The passage does not compare jazz with other music, and it stresses jazz's rules.

hints: What two things does the final paragraph say are needed?

strategy.explanation: Use the last paragraph to frame the whole passage.

candidates.remember: A main idea should include the passage's turn, not just its first lesson.

candidates.stem: When Mr. Okafor says, "That was free. It was not improvised," he most likely means that:

choices.A: the narrator had played too loudly to be heard over the recording.
choices.B: improvising requires the musician to plan every note in advance.
choices.C: ignoring the music's structure is not the same as improvising.
choices.D: the narrator should have played exactly what was on the recording.

candidates.evidence: They are working within a set of chords that repeat beneath the melody
candidates.explanation: The second paragraph explains the remark: improvisers work within the chords; the narrator's playing ignored them, so it was free but not improvised.

A.rationale: Volume is never the issue; the remark distinguishes two kinds of playing.

B.rationale: The passage says improvised solos are unrehearsed, like conversation.

D.rationale: Copying the recording would not be improvising either.

hints: How does the second paragraph explain the remark?

strategy.explanation: Read the remark together with the explanation that follows.

candidates.remember: When a remark puzzles the narrator, the next paragraph usually explains it.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must connect the remark to the later explanation and avoid the overstatement that improvising means planning.

candidates.stem: The comparison between a jazz solo and a conversation in the second paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that jazz solos are usually prepared in advance like speeches.
choices.B: show how a performance can be unrehearsed and still follow shared rules.
choices.C: explain why some musicians deliberately clash with the chords in a song.
choices.D: argue that listeners should talk with musicians during a performance.

candidates.evidence: the speakers have not rehearsed their words, yet they share a language
candidates.explanation: The analogy explains how a solo can be spontaneous yet structured: speakers don't rehearse words but share a language with rules.

A.rationale: The comparison stresses that neither the solo nor the conversation is rehearsed.

C.rationale: Clashing is mentioned earlier in the paragraph; the comparison concerns spontaneity within rules.

D.rationale: The comparison is a figure of speech, not advice to listeners.

hints: What do a solo and a conversation have in common, according to the passage?

strategy.explanation: Identify the two features the analogy pairs.

candidates.remember: An analogy's function is the shared feature it highlights.

author_checklist.hardness: One distractor borrows a detail from the same paragraph that the analogy does not address.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, transcribing a solo involved:

choices.A: memorizing a solo from sheet music written by the original musician.
choices.B: playing along with a recording until the solo felt natural.
choices.C: inventing new solos over the chords of a famous recording.
choices.D: slowing a recording down and writing out every note by ear.

candidates.evidence: listen to a recording of a great saxophonist, slow it down, and write out every note by ear
candidates.explanation: The third paragraph defines transcribing: listening to a recording, slowing it down, and writing out every note by ear.

A.rationale: The narrator worked by ear from recordings, not from sheet music.

B.rationale: Playing along was the first lesson, not transcription.

C.rationale: Transcribing meant copying a solo exactly, not inventing one.

hints: Find the dash in the third paragraph.

strategy.explanation: Read the definition after the dash.

candidates.remember: Definitions are often set off by a dash or a colon.

candidates.stem: Mr. Okafor's reply that "nobody ever learned to speak by inventing words" most strongly suggests that he believes:

choices.A: a personal style grows from what a musician learns from others.
choices.B: students should give up on trying to find a voice of their own.
choices.C: learning to speak is more difficult than learning to play music.
choices.D: copying the solos of great musicians is the final goal of study.

candidates.evidence: a voice is built from what it has absorbed
candidates.explanation: Okafor's answer pairs the image of learning words with the claim that a voice is built from what it absorbs: originality grows out of learned material.

B.rationale: He says a voice is built from what it absorbs, not that students should abandon it.

C.rationale: The comparison is about how both are learned, not which is harder.

D.rationale: He presents absorbing others' playing as the foundation of a voice, not the goal.

hints: What does Okafor say a voice is built from?

strategy.explanation: Read the whole reply in the third paragraph.

candidates.remember: Analogies in dialogue usually restate the speaker's claim in other terms.

candidates.stem: When the narrator says Mr. Okafor "was right, though not entirely," the narrator most likely means that:

choices.A: transcription took too long to be worth assigning to most students.
choices.B: absorbing other players' phrases alone did not produce a personal style.
choices.C: the narrator had already found a personal voice before transcribing.
choices.D: great saxophonists never learned by transcribing other musicians.

candidates.evidence: My solos were collages of borrowed phrases
candidates.explanation: Transcription gave the narrator the language (Okafor was right), but two years of it produced only imitations; a personal voice required something more (not entirely right).

C.rationale: The narrator's early playing was "free," not a voice.

D.rationale: Nothing in the passage says how great saxophonists learned.

hints: What could the narrator do after two years of transcribing, and what was missing?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentences after "though not entirely."

candidates.remember: A qualified judgment needs both its "right" part and its "not entirely" part.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must infer what the qualification refers to from the sentences that follow it.

candidates.stem: As it is used in the fourth paragraph, the word collages most nearly means:

choices.A: paintings made by gluing paper to canvas.
choices.B: exact imitations of a single musician.
choices.C: assemblages of pieces from other sources.
choices.D: brief summaries of longer pieces of music.

candidates.evidence: collages of borrowed phrases, stitched together
candidates.explanation: Solos that were "collages of borrowed phrases, stitched together" were assemblies of pieces taken from other players.

A.rationale: That is the literal art meaning, not the figurative one here.

B.rationale: The solos drew on half a dozen musicians, combined, not one copied exactly.

D.rationale: The solos were pieced together, not shortened.

hints: What are the solos made of, according to the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Predict a meaning from "borrowed phrases, stitched together."

candidates.remember: For figurative words, use the sentence's own description.

candidates.stem: The narrator describes the solo played after forgetting a memorized phrase as "mine" mainly because the narrator:

choices.A: played it more smoothly than any of the solos learned by transcribing.
choices.B: received praise from Mr. Okafor for playing it at a performance.
choices.C: had stopped transcribing other musicians' solos some time before.
choices.D: had to find a way back to the chord without relying on a borrowed phrase.

candidates.evidence: had to find my own way back to the chord
candidates.explanation: Forgetting the memorized phrase forced the narrator to invent a path back to the chord, so the result, though clumsy, was the narrator's own.

C.rationale: Nothing says the narrator stopped transcribing at that point.

hints: What did the narrator have to do after forgetting the phrase?

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence just before "What I played was clumsy."

candidates.remember: Look for the cause stated right before a key claim.

author_checklist.hardness: The tempting distractor equates "mine" with "better played," which the passage contradicts.

candidates.stem: The last sentence of the passage mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that students should try to make as many mistakes as possible.
choices.B: argue that personal expression requires departing from learned material.
choices.C: explain why the narrator stopped assigning transcriptions to students.
choices.D: argue that learned material is more important than personal expression.

candidates.evidence: Without the occasional mistake that forces you off the script, there is no one saying it.
candidates.explanation: The last sentence completes the pair: learned language gives something to say, and departures from it supply a person saying it.

A.rationale: The narrator speaks of an occasional mistake, not as many as possible.

D.rationale: The final two sentences treat both as necessary.

hints: How does the last sentence pair with the one before it?

strategy.explanation: Read the final two sentences together.

candidates.remember: Paired closing sentences often state the two sides of a balanced conclusion.

candidates.stem: The narrator's current attitude toward transcription is best described as:

choices.A: treating it as the only reliable way for students to learn.
choices.B: regretting the years spent on it as largely wasted effort.
choices.C: valuing it as necessary, though not enough by itself.
choices.D: doubting whether it helps students who want to improvise.

candidates.evidence: I teach now, and I still assign transcriptions.
candidates.explanation: The narrator still assigns transcriptions but also tells students that departing from learned material is needed: necessary but not sufficient.

A.rationale: The narrator also teaches the lesson of departing from it.

B.rationale: The narrator still assigns it and credits it with providing the language.

D.rationale: The narrator still assigns it because it teaches the language.

hints: What does the narrator still do, and what does the narrator add?

strategy.explanation: Test each attitude against the final paragraph.

candidates.remember: Attitude answers must fit everything the author does, not one sentence.

candidates.stem: Passage B's final sentence most directly challenges which proposal from Passage A?

choices.A: That parking spaces in garages are expensive to build.
choices.B: That eliminating parking minimums is the right policy for every city.
choices.C: That minimum parking rules were meant to keep cars off streets.
choices.D: That several cities have recently eliminated their minimums.

candidates.evidence: uniform rules are exactly what got cities into trouble in the first place
candidates.explanation: Passage B's last sentence warns that eliminating minimums everywhere replaces one uniform rule with another, challenging Passage A's single approach.

A.rationale: Passage B never disputes the cost of garages.

C.rationale: Passage B does not discuss why minimums were adopted.

D.rationale: Passage B does not dispute that this happened.

strategy.explanation: Match the final sentence to Passage A's recommendation.

candidates.remember: A closing sentence often targets the opposing passage's main recommendation.

revision_history.reason: solver: Passage A never says one approach fits every neighborhood; key reworded to the elimination proposal Passage B attacks

candidates.author_reason: withdrawn: R054-10 revision 2 introduced a stem cue (key the only choice worded as a proposal); rewording the other choices as proposals would risk a second defensible answer, so the item is retired rather than revised again
